questions.question: Define tension and compression, state which of rope, brick, steel and timber carries each well, and describe how you could tell which force a member is carrying.
questions.expected_answer: Tension is a member being pulled from both ends so that it tends to stretch; compression is a member being pushed from both ends so that it tends to shorten or buckle. Rope carries tension only; a stack of bricks carries compression only; steel carries both and is excellent in tension; timber and concrete carry both but are better in compression. Imagine cutting the member: in tension the cut ends spring apart, in compression they press together. In drawings tension arrows point outward along the member and compression arrows point inward.

questions.question: Name the members of a roof truss and state whether each is in tension or compression, explaining the job of the tie beam.
questions.expected_answer: Rafters (top chords): the sloping members carrying the roof load down to the walls, in compression. Tie beam (bottom chord): the horizontal member joining the rafter feet, in tension; it stops the rafters spreading and pushing the walls outward so the walls receive only vertical load. Struts: web members in compression that hold the rafters up at mid-span. Ties: web members in tension that pull points together. Post: the vertical from apex to tie beam, in tension in king and queen post trusses because it hangs the tie beam from the apex.

questions.question: Compare the king post and queen post trusses: describe their members, the force in each post and straining beam, and the span each suits.
questions.expected_answer: King post: two rafters, a tie beam, one central vertical king post from apex to tie beam centre (tension, holding up the tie beam), and two struts from its foot to the rafters (compression); suits spans of about 5-8 m, a typical house. Queen post: two rafters, a tie beam, two vertical queen posts a third of the way in from each end (tension, holding up the tie beam at two points), a horizontal straining beam between their tops (compression, keeping them apart), and struts to the rafters; suits spans of about 8-12 m, such as halls and classrooms.
